{{Short description|Chordal graph where all cycles of even length have odd chords}}

[[File:Strongly chordal graphs.svg|thumb|400px|In the first graph, the 8-cycle has odd edges 3-6 and 2-7, and the 6-cycles each also have one of those two edges as an odd edge.

In the second graph, although the graph without the red edge is [[chordal graph|chordal]], the red edge must be added to make an odd chord for the 6-cycle formed by all vertices excluding 4 and 5.]]

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] area of [[graph theory]], an [[undirected graph]] {{mvar|G}} is '''strongly chordal''' if it is a [[chordal graph]] and every [[cycle (graph theory)|cycle]] of even length (≥ 6) in {{mvar|G}} has an ''odd chord'', i.e., an edge that connects two [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] that are an odd [[Distance (graph theory)|distance]] (>1) apart from each other in the cycle.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Le|Spinrad|1999}}, Definition 3.4.1, p. 43.</ref>

==Characterizations==
Strongly chordal graphs have a [[Forbidden graph characterization|forbidden subgraph characterization]] as the graphs that do not contain an induced cycle of length greater than three or an [[n-sun|''n''-sun]] (''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;3) as an [[induced subgraph]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Chang|1982}}; {{harvtxt|Farber|1983}}; {{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Le|Spinrad|1999}}, Theorem 7.2.1, p. 112.</ref> An ''n''-sun is a chordal graph with 2''n'' vertices, partitioned into two subsets ''U''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{''u''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''u''<sub>2</sub>,...} and ''W''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{''w''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''w''<sub>2</sub>,...}, such that each vertex ''w<sub>i</sub>'' in ''W'' has exactly two neighbors, ''u''<sub>''i''</sub> and ''u''<sub>(''i''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)&nbsp;mod&nbsp;''n''</sub>. An ''n''-sun cannot be strongly chordal, because the cycle ''u''<sub>1</sub>''w''<sub>1</sub>''u''<sub>2</sub>''w''<sub>2</sub>... has no odd chord.

Strongly chordal graphs may also be characterized as the graphs having a strong perfect elimination ordering, an ordering of the vertices such that the neighbors of any vertex that come later in the ordering form a [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] and such that, for each ''i''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''j''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''l'', if the ''i''th vertex in the ordering is adjacent to the ''k''th and the ''l''th vertices, and the ''j''th and ''k''th vertices are adjacent, then the ''j''th and ''l''th vertices must also be adjacent.<ref>{{harvtxt|Farber|1983}}; {{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Le|Spinrad|1999}}, Theorem 5.5.1, p. 77.</ref>

A graph is strongly chordal [[if and only if]] every one of its induced subgraphs has a simple vertex, a vertex whose neighbors have neighborhoods that are linearly ordered by inclusion.<ref>{{harvtxt|Farber|1983}}; {{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Le|Spinrad|1999}}, Theorem 5.5.2, p. 78.</ref> Also, a graph is strongly chordal if and only if it is chordal and every cycle of length five or more has a 2-chord triangle, a triangle formed by two chords and an edge of the cycle.<ref>{{harvtxt|Dahlhaus|Manuel|Miller|1998}}.</ref>

A graph is strongly chordal if and only if each of its induced subgraphs is a [[dually chordal graph]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Dragan|Chepoi|Voloshin|1998}}, Corollary 3, p. 444</ref>

Strongly chordal graphs may also be characterized in terms of the number of [[clique (graph theory)|complete subgraphs]] each edge participates in.<ref>{{harvtxt|McKee|1999}}</ref>
Yet another characterization is given in.<ref>{{harvtxt|De Caria|McKee|2014}}</ref>

==Recognition==
It is possible to determine whether a graph is strongly chordal in [[polynomial time]], by repeatedly searching for and removing a simple vertex. If this process eliminates all vertices in the graph, the graph must be strongly chordal; otherwise, if this process finds a subgraph without any more simple vertices, the original graph cannot be strongly chordal. For a strongly chordal graph, the order in which the vertices are removed by this process is a strong perfect elimination ordering.<ref>{{harvtxt|Farber|1983}}.</ref>

Alternative algorithms are now known that can determine whether a graph is strongly chordal and, if so, construct a strong perfect elimination ordering more efficiently, in time {{nowrap|O(min(''n''<sup>2</sup>, (''n'' + ''m'') log ''n''))}} for a graph with ''n'' vertices and ''m'' edges.<ref>{{harvtxt|Lubiw|1987}}; {{harvtxt|Paige|Tarjan|1987}}; {{harvtxt|Spinrad|1993}}.</ref>

==Subclasses==
An important subclass (based on [[phylogeny]]) is the class of {{mvar|k}}-[[leaf power]]s, the graphs formed from the leaves of a tree by connecting two leaves by an edge when their distance in the tree is at most {{mvar|k}}. A leaf power is a graph that is a {{mvar|k}}-leaf power for some {{mvar|k}}.
Since powers of strongly chordal graphs are strongly chordal and trees are strongly chordal, it follows that leaf powers are strongly chordal. They form a proper subclass of strongly chordal graphs,
which in turn includes the [[cluster graph]]s as the 2-leaf powers.<ref>{{harvtxt|Nishimura|Ragde|Thilikos|2002}}</ref>
Another important subclass of strongly chordal graphs are [[interval graph]]s. In <ref>{{harvtxt|Brandstädt|Hundt|Mancini|Wagner|2010}}</ref> it is shown that interval graphs and the larger class of rooted directed path graphs are leaf powers.

==Algorithmic problems==

Since strongly chordal graphs are both [[chordal graph]]s and [[dually chordal graph]]s, various NP-complete problems such as Independent Set, Clique, Coloring, [[Clique cover|Clique Cover]], [[Dominating set|Dominating Set]], and Steiner Tree can be solved efficiently for strongly chordal graphs. Graph isomorphism is isomorphism-complete for strongly chordal graphs.<ref>{{harvtxt|Uehara|Toda|Nagoya|2005}}</ref> 
Hamiltonian Circuit remains NP-complete for strongly chordal [[split graph]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Müller|1996}}</ref>
